prompt: The complex numbers $x,y,z$ satisfy $$\begin{aligned}xyz&=-4\\(x+1)(y+1)(z+1)&=7\\(x+2)(y+2)(z+2)&=-3.\end{aligned}$$ Find, with proof, the value of $(x+3)(y+3)(z+3)$.

solutions.title: Finite differences of a monic cubic
solutions.body:
Let $f(t)=(x+t)(y+t)(z+t)$, a monic cubic in $t$. For any cubic with leading coefficient $1$ the third finite difference is $3!=6$: $f(3)-3f(2)+3f(1)-f(0)=6$. Hence $f(3)=6+3f(2)-3f(1)+f(0)=6+3(-3)-3(7)+(-4)=-28$.

**Answer: $-28$**

solutions.title: Solve for the symmetric functions
solutions.body: Let $u=x+y+z$, $v=xy+yz+zx$, $w=xyz$. The three equations read $w=-4$, $w+v+u+1=7$, $w+2v+4u+8=-3$, a linear system with solution $u=-\frac{27}2$, $v=\frac{47}2$, $w=-4$. Then $(x+3)(y+3)(z+3)=w+3v+9u+27=-4+\frac{141}2-\frac{243}2+27=-28$.

prompt: Let $P$ be a (non-self-intersecting) polygon in the plane. Let $C_1,\ldots,C_n$ be circles in the plane whose interiors cover the interior of $P$. For $1\le i\le n$, let $r_i$ be the radius of $C_i$. Prove that there is a single circle of radius $r_1+\cdots+r_n$ whose interior covers the interior of $P$.
answer: Induct on $n$: if two of the discs overlap, replace them by one disc of radius $r_i+r_j$ containing both.

solutions.title: Merge overlapping discs
solutions.body: Induct on $n$. If $n=1$ there is nothing to prove. Let $n>1$. The interior of $P$ is connected and nonempty and is covered by the open discs. If the open discs were pairwise disjoint, then $\operatorname{int}P$ (connected) would lie in a single one, say $C_k$, and the concentric circle of radius $r_1+\cdots+r_n\ge r_k$ covers it. Otherwise two open discs $C_i,C_j$ overlap, so $d=O_iO_j<r_i+r_j$. Choose a point $O$ on segment $O_iO_j$ with $O_iO\le r_j$ and $O_jO\le r_i$ (possible: take $O_iO=t$ with $\max(0,d-r_i)\le t\le\min(d,r_j)$, a nonempty range since $d<r_i+r_j$). The circle $C$ centred at $O$ with radius $r_i+r_j$ contains $C_i$ (as $OO_i+r_i\le r_j+r_i$) and $C_j$ (as $OO_j+r_j\le r_i+r_j$). Replace $C_i,C_j$ by $C$: this gives $n-1$ circles with the same total radius whose interiors still cover $\operatorname{int}P$. By induction there is a single circle of radius $r_1+\cdots+r_n$ covering $\operatorname{int}P$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $z=a+bi$ be a complex number with integer real and imaginary parts $a,b\in\mathbb Z$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$ (i.e. $z$ is a Gaussian integer). If $p$ is an odd prime number, show that the real part of $z^p-z$ is an integer divisible by $p$.

solutions.title: Binomial expansion and Fermat
solutions.body: By the binomial theorem, $$\operatorname{Re}(z^p)=\sum_{k\text{ even}}\binom pk(-1)^{k/2}a^{p-k}b^k=a^p-\binom p2a^{p-2}b^2+\binom p4a^{p-4}b^4-\cdots.$$ Since $p$ is odd, $k$ ranges over even numbers $0\le k\le p-1$, and for $2\le k\le p-1$ the coefficient $\binom pk$ is divisible by $p$. So $\operatorname{Re}(z^p)\equiv a^p\pmod p$, and by Fermat's little theorem $a^p\equiv a$. Hence $\operatorname{Re}(z^p-z)=\operatorname{Re}(z^p)-a\equiv0\pmod p$. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
(Convex) quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $BC=CD$ is inscribed in circle $\Omega$; the diagonals of $ABCD$ meet at $X$. Suppose $AD<AB$, the circumcircle of triangle $BCX$ intersects segment $AB$ at a point $Y\ne B$, and ray $\overrightarrow{CY}$ meets $\Omega$ again at a point $Z\ne C$. Prove that ray $\overrightarrow{DY}$ bisects angle $ZDB$.

(We have only included the conditions $AD<AB$ and that $Z$ lies on ray $\overrightarrow{CY}$ for everyone's convenience. With slight modifications, the problem holds in general. But we will only grade your team's solution in this special case.)

solutions.title: Angle chase: $Y$ is the incenter of $ZDB$
solutions.body:
In this configuration $Y$ lies on segment $AB$ and $Z$ on the arc $AB$, so $Y$ is inside triangle $ZDB$. We show $BY$ and $ZY$ are angle bisectors of $\triangle ZDB$; then $Y$ is its incenter and $DY$ bisects $\angle ZDB$.

**$ZY$ bisects $\angle BZD$.** $CB=CD$, so the arcs $BC$ and $CD$ of $\Omega$ are equal, and the inscribed angles satisfy $\angle BZC=\angle CZD$. Since $Y$ lies on $ZC$, line $ZY$ bisects $\angle BZD$.

**$BY$ bisects $\angle DBZ$.** $X$ lies on $BD$ and on $CA$, and $Y$ lies on $BA$ and on $CZ$. Using the circle $BCXY$ and then $\Omega$: $$\angle DBA=\angle XBY=\angle XCY=\angle ACZ=\angle ABZ,$$ where $\angle XBY=\angle XCY$ are inscribed angles on chord $XY$ of circle $(BCXY)$ and $\angle ACZ=\angle ABZ$ are inscribed angles on chord $AZ$ of $\Omega$. So line $BA$ (that is, $BY$) bisects $\angle DBZ$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: For a convex quadrilateral $P$, let $D$ denote the sum of the lengths of its diagonals and let $S$ denote its perimeter. Determine, with proof, all possible values of $\frac SD$.
answer: All real numbers $\frac SD$ with $1<\frac SD<2$ (the open interval $(1,2)$).

solutions.title: Bounds by the triangle inequality, then constructions
solutions.body:
Let $ABCD$ be convex with diagonals $AC,BD$ meeting at $E$ (interior to both diagonals).

**$S>D$.** $AB+BC>AC$ and $AD+DC>AC$, so $S>2AC$; similarly $S>2BD$. Adding, $2S>2(AC+BD)$, so $S>D$.

**$S<2D$.** In triangles $AEB,BEC,CED,DEA$: $AE+EB>AB$, $BE+EC>BC$, $CE+ED>CD$, $DE+EA>DA$. Adding: $2(AE+EC+BE+ED)>S$, and $AE+EC=AC$, $BE+ED=BD$ give $2D>S$.

**Every value in $(1,2)$ occurs.** *Rectangles* with sides $1,x$ ($0<x\le1$): $S=2+2x$, $D=2\sqrt{1+x^2}$, $\frac SD=\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$, continuous in $x$, equal to $\sqrt2$ at $x=1$ and tending to $1$ as $x\to0^+$; by continuity it takes every value in $(1,\sqrt2]$. *Rhombi* with side $1$ and half-angle $\theta\in(0,45^\circ]$ at the vertex $B$ (so $AC=2\sin\theta$, $BD=2\cos\theta$): $S=4$, $D=2(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)$, $\frac SD=\frac2{\sin\theta+\cos\theta}$, equal to $\sqrt2$ at $45^\circ$ and tending to $2$ as $\theta\to0$; so it takes every value in $[\sqrt2,2)$.

Therefore the possible values are exactly those in $(1,2)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Sindy has 100 dollars in pennies (worth 0.01 dollars each), nickels (worth 0.05 each), dimes (worth 0.10 each), and quarters (worth 0.25 each). Prove that she can split her coins into two piles, each with total value exactly 50 dollars.
answer: Reduce to nickels, dimes, quarters; fill one pile greedily.

solutions.title: Reduce, then greedy with a nickel fix-up
solutions.body:
Work in units of $5$ cents. Since every coin except pennies is worth a multiple of $5$ cents and the total is $10000$ cents, the number of pennies is a multiple of $5$; group them in fives, each group acting as a nickel (never separated). Now we have $q$ quarters (value $5$), $d$ dimes (value $2$) and $n$ nickels (value $1$) with $5q+2d+n=2000$, and we want to split into two piles of value $1000$.

If $q\ge200$, put $200$ quarters in one pile; if $d\ge500$, put $500$ dimes; if $n\ge1000$, put $1000$ nickels: the pile has value $1000$ and the rest has value $1000$. So assume $q\le199$, $d\le499$, $n\le999$. Then $5q+2d\le995+998<2000$, so $n\ge1$.

Put all quarters in pile $1$ (value $5q\le995$). Add dimes one at a time.
- If the value reaches exactly $1000$, done.
- If it jumps from $999$ to $1001$, remove that last dime and add a nickel instead (a nickel is available since $n\ge1$): the value is $1000$.
- If the dimes run out before reaching $1000$, pile $1$ has all quarters and dimes, with value $5q+2d<1000$; add nickels one at a time. Since all the coins have total value $2000$, the number of nickels is $n=2000-5q-2d>1000$, so adding nickels one at a time reaches exactly $1000$.

In every case pile $1$ has value $1000$ units $=50$ dollars, and the remaining coins have value $50$ dollars. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb C$ be a nonconstant complex-valued function on the real interval $[0,1]$. Prove that there exists $\epsilon>0$ (possibly depending on $f$) such that for any polynomial $P$ with complex coefficients, there exists a complex number $z$ with $|z|\le1$ such that $|f(|z|)-P(z)|\ge\epsilon$.
answer: Take $\epsilon=\frac12|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|$ for $x_1,x_2$ with $f(x_1)\ne f(x_2)$; average $P$ over a circle (roots-of-unity filter).

solutions.title: Roots-of-unity filter
solutions.body:
Since $f$ is not constant, pick $x_1,x_2\in[0,1]$ with $f(x_1)\ne f(x_2)$ and put $\epsilon=\frac12|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|>0$. Suppose, for contradiction, that some polynomial $P$ satisfies $|f(|z|)-P(z)|<\epsilon$ for all $|z|\le1$.

Fix $r\in[0,1]$ and a prime $q>\deg P$. Apply the inequality at $z_k=re^{2\pi ik/q}$ ($k=0,\ldots,q-1$), all with $|z_k|=r$: $|f(r)-P(z_k)|<\epsilon$. Averaging and using the triangle inequality, $$\left|f(r)-\frac1q\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}P(z_k)\right|<\epsilon.$$ For $P(z)=\sum_jc_jz^j$ with $j<q$, $\frac1q\sum_kz_k^j=r^j\cdot\frac1q\sum_ke^{2\pi ijk/q}$ equals $0$ for $1\le j<q$ and $1$ for $j=0$; so the average is $c_0=P(0)$. Hence $|f(r)-P(0)|<\epsilon$ for every $r\in[0,1]$. Taking $r=x_1$ and $r=x_2$ and subtracting, $|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<2\epsilon=|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|$, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,2015\}$. With proof, determine the maximum possible number of ordered pairs $(i,j)\in\{1,2,\ldots,2015\}^2$ with $i<j$ such that $\pi(i)\cdot\pi(j)>i\cdot j$.

solutions.title: Construction and an Ore-type upper bound
solutions.body:
Let $n=2015$ and call $(i,j)$, $i<j$, *good* if $\pi(i)\pi(j)>ij$. We show the maximum is $\binom{n-1}2=2027091$.

**Construction.** $\pi(k)=k+1$ for $k<n$ and $\pi(n)=1$. For $i<j\le n-1$: $\pi(i)\pi(j)=(i+1)(j+1)>ij$, so all $\binom{n-1}2$ pairs among $1,\ldots,n-1$ are good.

**Upper bound.** Put $z_i=\pi(i)/i>0$; then $\prod_{i}z_i=1$. Let $G$ be the graph on $[n]$ with $i\sim j$ iff $z_iz_j>1$ (good pairs). If $C=(v_1,\ldots,v_k)$ is a cycle in $G$, then $1<\prod_{t}z_{v_t}z_{v_{t+1}}=\prod_{v\in C}z_v^2$, so $\prod_{v\in C}z_v>1$. In particular $G$ has no Hamiltonian cycle (else $\prod z_i>1$). By Ore's theorem (if $d(u)+d(v)\ge n$ for all non-adjacent $u,v$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian), there are non-adjacent $u,v$ with $d(u)+d(v)\le n-1$. Then $|E|\le\binom{n-2}2+(n-1)=\binom{n-1}2+1$.

Suppose equality. Then $G-\{u,v\}$ is complete and $d(u)+d(v)=n-1$. As $u\not\sim v$, $d(u),d(v)\le n-2$, so both are $\ge1$, and since $n-1\ge5$ one of them, say $d(u)$, is $\ge3$. Let $w$ be a neighbour of $v$ and $a,b,c$ three neighbours of $u$; choose $a,b\ne w$. $G-\{u,v,w\}$ is complete and contains $a,b$, so it has a Hamiltonian path from $a$ to $b$; closing it through $u$ gives a cycle $C$ through all vertices except $v,w$. Then $\prod_{x\in C}z_x>1$ and $z_vz_w>1$ ($v\sim w$), so $\prod_{i=1}^nz_i>1$, a contradiction. Hence $|E|\le\binom{n-1}2$.

The maximum is $\binom{2014}2=2027091$.

**Answer: 2027091**

prompt: Let $z=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{101}}$ and let $\omega=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{10}}$. Prove that $$\prod_{a=0}^9\prod_{b=0}^{100}\prod_{c=0}^{100}\left(\omega^a+z^b+z^c\right)$$ is an integer and find (with proof) its remainder upon division by $101$.

solutions.title: Galois invariance and the Frobenius congruence
solutions.body:
Let $\Pi$ denote the product, $p=101$, $r=10$.

**$\Pi$ is an integer.** $\Pi$ is an algebraic integer. Every automorphism of $\mathbb Q(\omega,z)$ sends $\omega\mapsto\omega^k$, $z\mapsto z^l$ ($\gcd(k,10)=\gcd(l,101)=1$), which permutes the factors $(\omega^a+z^b+z^c)$ (permuting $a,b,c$ by the bijections $a\mapsto ka$, $b\mapsto lb$, $c\mapsto lc$). So $\Pi$ is fixed by the Galois group, hence rational, hence an integer.

**Remainder mod $p$.** Work in $R=\mathbb Z[\omega,z]$ (algebraic integers), writing $\alpha\equiv\beta$ if $(\alpha-\beta)/p\in R$. Then $(u+v)^p\equiv u^p+v^p$. For fixed $a,b$ put $x=-\omega^a-z^b$; since $\prod_c(x-z^c)=x^p-1$ and $p$ is odd, $$\prod_c(\omega^a+z^b+z^c)=(-1)^p\prod_c(x-z^c)=-(x^p-1).$$ By the Frobenius congruence $x^p\equiv-(\omega^{pa}+z^{pb})=-(\omega^{pa}+1)$ (as $z^{pb}=1$), so $-(x^p-1)\equiv\omega^{pa}+2$. This does not depend on $b$, so taking the product over $b$: $\prod_{b,c}\equiv(\omega^{pa}+2)^p\equiv\omega^{p^2a}+2^p\equiv\omega^{a}+2$, because $p=101\equiv1\pmod{10}$ (so $\omega^{p^2a}=\omega^a$) and $2^p\equiv2$ (Fermat). Therefore $$\Pi\equiv\prod_{a=0}^9(\omega^a+2)=\prod_a(-1)(-2-\omega^a)=(-2)^{10}-1=1023,$$ using $\prod_a(x-\omega^a)=x^{10}-1$ at $x=-2$. Since $\Pi-1023$ is an integer divisible by $p$ in $R$, it is divisible by $p$ in $\mathbb Z$. Thus $\Pi\equiv1023\equiv13\pmod{101}$.

**Answer: 13**

prompt: The sequences of real numbers $\{a_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ and $\{b_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ satisfy $a_{n+1}=(a_{n-1}-1)(b_n+1)$ and $b_{n+1}=a_nb_{n-1}-1$ for $n\ge2$, with $a_1=a_2=2015$ and $b_1=b_2=2013$. Evaluate, with proof, the infinite sum $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\left(\frac1{a_{n+1}}-\frac1{a_{n+3}}\right).$$

solutions.title: Telescoping
solutions.body:
**Growth.** By induction $a_n,b_n\ge2013$ and both sequences are nondecreasing ($a_3=2014^2$, $b_3=2015\cdot2013-1$ exceed $a_2,b_2$, and $a_{n+1}=(a_{n-1}-1)(b_n+1)\ge(a_{n-2}-1)(b_{n-1}+1)=a_n$, similarly for $b$); moreover $a_{n+1}\ge2014\,(a_{n-1}-1)\ge2a_{n-1}$, so $a_n\to\infty$. In particular no denominator below vanishes.

**Key identity.** For $n\ge1$: $b_{n+2}+1=a_{n+1}b_n$, so $a_{n+3}=(a_{n+1}-1)(b_{n+2}+1)=a_{n+1}(a_{n+1}-1)b_n$. Hence $$\frac{b_n}{a_{n+3}}=\frac1{a_{n+1}(a_{n+1}-1)}=\frac1{a_{n+1}-1}-\frac1{a_{n+1}},$$ and the $n$-th term is $$t_n=\frac{b_n}{a_{n+1}}-\frac1{a_{n+1}-1}+\frac1{a_{n+1}}=\frac{b_n+1}{a_{n+1}}-\frac1{a_{n+1}-1}.$$ For $n\ge2$, $b_n+1=\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n-1}-1}$, so $t_n=\frac1{a_{n-1}-1}-\frac1{a_{n+1}-1}$, which telescopes: $$\sum_{n\ge2}t_n=\frac1{a_1-1}+\frac1{a_2-1}-\lim_{N\to\infty}\left(\frac1{a_N-1}+\frac1{a_{N+1}-1}\right)=\frac2{2014}.$$ The first term is $t_1=\frac{b_1+1}{a_2}-\frac1{a_2-1}=\frac{2014}{2015}-\frac1{2014}$. Total: $\frac{2014}{2015}-\frac1{2014}+\frac2{2014}=1-\frac1{2015}+\frac1{2014}=1+\frac1{2014\cdot2015}=\frac{4058211}{4058210}$.

**Answer: $1+\frac1{2014\cdot2015}=\frac{4058211}{4058210}$**
